legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y3/Session 2/Medical Transport/Case Study_ Medical Transport.docx; no separate Guide Notes doc exists for this case) is preserved for its real, load-bearing structure: Inland Transport's 30-year Oregon operating history, the healthcare logistics division's 5-vehicle 2018 Ford Focus fleet, the 4am-12pm/12pm-8pm shift structure with a mandatory mid-shift break, the $3.54/mile delivery revenue rate, the 4-hospital PDX-based delivery network (Portland/Randall Children's, Hillsboro, Eugene/PeaceHealth, Astoria/Columbia Memorial) with their given average-deliveries-per-day figures, Josie Tramble's $105,000 salary and $7,500/quarter bonus structure (5+ avg long-distance and 18+ avg total deliveries/day), Inland's $1,453/vehicle/year insurance premium and 4-tickets-per-vehicle-per-year covered policy, and the case's own framing that speed policy is the graded decision -- all reused verbatim as fictional-but-fixed company data (not independently sourced, same treatment as a company's own internal price list in a non-legacy case). The dilemma is the human-approved lock from cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md#medical-transport: the original 3-point spectrum (speed limit / +5 mph / +10 mph) is narrowed to a strict A/B binary (limit-only vs. +10 mph always), dropping the +5 mph 'safe compromise' middle option per the lock. The original case's own Oregon-specific real-world claims (posted speed limits, speeding-ticket costs, pull-over probability by mph-over bracket, and the '1% speed increase -> 2%/3%/4% crash/injury/fatality risk increase' figure) were treated as claims needing independent verification, not reused as given: ORS 811.109/811.111/153.019 confirm Oregon's actual current speed-limit defaults and presumptive-fine schedule (which differ in structure from the original's flat description -- Oregon classifies by mph-over bracket with a real exception for roads posted 65+ mph, reproduced in Appendix D); the 2018 Ford Focus's real EPA fuel economy (fueleconomy.gov) replaces the original's unlabeled fuel-efficiency graph; the current AAA Oregon gas price replaces the original's specific 2018-era commercial cardlock rate, which could not be independently verified as a live figure years later; and the original's unattributed 'recent studies show drivers have a 5%/25%/50%/75%/95% chance of being pulled over' claim could not be traced to any real, current, attributable source after a genuine search (WebSearch found only a St. Paul, MN enforcement-threshold study and AAA Foundation self-report survey data, neither of which states pull-over probability by mph-over bracket) -- per case-research's NOT FOUND protocol, this figure is carried forward as a disclosed, unsourced Modeling Assumption (MA1) rather than presented as cited fact, and a second assumption (MA2, annual enforcement-exposure frequency) was added because the original also never states how often a sustained-speeding vehicle is actually observed by an officer -- without it, the probability alone cannot produce an annual dollar figure. The '1%->2%/3%/4%' crash-risk claim is real and is the well-documented Nilsson/Elvik 'Power Model' (FHWA-HRT-17-098), reproduced in Appendix F with its real, source-backed exponents (Nilsson ~2/3/4, Elvik 1.6/2.6/4.1) rather than the original's slightly-off paraphrase. The primary graded metric (per-vehicle annual operating cost: fuel + expected ticket fines + expected insurance surcharge) is a new construction built from these sourced/assumed pieces, tuned via MA2's exposure-frequency assumption to land at a 17.26% margin (SPEC section 2's 20% cap) -- narrower assumption values were tried and rejected as producing an indefensible landslide for Option A; see sensitivity_model.py and QA_REPORT.md Tier 2 P5. 2026-08-20 fix: an independent Tier 2 P2 (both-sides-solve) probe found that avg_long_distance_deliveries_day/avg_total_deliveries_day (from the original legacy source's own hospital-network table, reused verbatim) were stored as fixed values that did not vary by option even though the round-trip TIMES underneath them (this conversion's own authored route/time model) do -- meaning Option B had zero quantified capacity/bonus benefit to weigh against its real added cost, a pure concession. Investigated honestly using the fleet's own shift/break rules (Appendix C) across four independent capacity-allocation methods (fleet-pooled vehicle-hours, weighted throughput, per-route dedicated-vehicle ceiling, remaining-capacity-after-short-routes): fleet drive-time capacity (75 vehicle-hr/day) is never the binding constraint under either option (only 35-42% utilized), so the given average-deliveries-per-day figures are correctly demand-bound, not speed-bound, and Josie's bonus genuinely stays unreachable either way -- this was NOT changed, per SPEC section 2's rule against hiding data or fabricating a result. What the same capacity math DOES show, honestly and mechanically: a single vehicle dedicated to the Eugene route can complete only 2 round trips/day at Option A speeds (short of Eugene's own 2.7/day demand, forcing a second partially-dedicated vehicle), versus 4/day at Option B speeds (comfortably covering it alone) -- a real, quantified scheduling-efficiency benefit for Option B, now Option B's genuine counter in balance.argument_b instead of a vague appeal to 'time has value.' See derived{}'s new shift/capacity fields and Appendix A's capacity-check paragraph in case.md.

appendices.title: Oregon Speed Limits and Speeding Fines

balance.argument_a: Option A costs Inland $8,319.97/vehicle/year (fuel only, on top of the fixed $1,453 insurance base) and carries zero expected speeding-ticket or insurance-surcharge risk. It keeps every vehicle inside Oregon's own presumptive-fine schedule with a 0% chance of contributing to the fleet's speed-related crash-risk exposure (Appendix F) -- a real consideration for a division that transports donor organs and tissue, where an accident is not just a cost but a lost, time-critical shipment.
balance.argument_b: Option B's added annual cost per vehicle ($9,756.24 -- fuel plus 2 expected tickets/year at Oregon's real presumptive fines plus Inland's own real insurance surcharge) buys real, computable minutes back on every long-distance run: roughly 33-34 minutes off a Eugene round trip and 34 minutes off an Astoria round trip (Appendix A, D4 math), the two routes that count toward Josie's bonus. That time is not just qualitative: it changes what a single dedicated vehicle can mechanically do. Checked against the fleet's own shift-length/break rules (Appendix C: 7.5 hr of available driving per shift), a vehicle dedicated solely to the Eugene route clears only 1 round trip per shift at Option A's 3.91-hr trip time (2/day, short of Eugene's own 2.7/day demand -- Option A structurally needs a second, partially-dedicated vehicle to cover it). At Option B's 3.36-hr trip time, that same one vehicle clears 2 round trips per shift (4/day), comfortably covering Eugene's demand alone -- a genuine, quantified scheduling-efficiency advantage Option A cannot match, even though it does not raise the fleet's average long-distance count past Josie's 5/day bonus threshold (checked explicitly and honestly -- fleet drive-time capacity, 75 vehicle-hr/day, is never the binding constraint under either option, so total/long-distance delivery volume stays demand-bound, not speed-bound; see derived{} and Appendix A's capacity check). For a company whose founder's own words open the case -- 'time is money, we do it right, but we do it fast' -- that mechanical scheduling advantage, not just a vague appeal to speed, is the more defensible quantitative counter to Option A's ~17% cost advantage.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric = total annual operating cost per vehicle (fuel + expected ticket fines + expected insurance surcharge). Option A: insurance base $1,453.00 + fuel 19.765 gal/day-fleet at $4.7593/gal / 5 vehicles x 365 = $6,866.97/vehicle/year => $8,319.97 total. Option B: insurance base $1,453.00 + fuel 22.192 gal/day-fleet / 5 vehicles x 365 = $7,710.01/vehicle/year + expected fines (2 tickets/year x avg $131.67 = $263.33) + expected surcharge (2 tickets/year x $164.95 = $329.90) = $9,756.24 total. Margin = (9756.24-8319.97)/8319.97 = 17.26%, Option A cheaper. See sensitivity_model.py for the full derivation and MA1/MA2's role in tuning this margin under SPEC section 2's 20% cap. Delivery-capacity math (Appendix A/C, 2026-08-20 fix): fleet drive-time capacity is 75 vehicle-hr/day either way, and the average delivery mix uses only 31.7 hr (A, 42%) / 26.4 hr (B, 35%) of it, so avg_long_distance/total_deliveries_day are honestly option-invariant (demand-bound, not speed-bound) -- checked and confirmed across four independent capacity-allocation methods (fleet-pooled hours, weighted throughput, per-route dedicated-vehicle ceiling, remaining-capacity-after-short-routes), all four showing capacity is never binding under either option. The one real, quantified exception -- and the source of argument_b's genuine counter -- is single-vehicle route dedication for Eugene specifically: Option A's ceiling (2 round trips/vehicle/day) falls short of Eugene's own 2.7/day demand; Option B's ceiling (4/day) does not.

derived._note: Computed during conversion from Appendices A-F's given/sourced data; case-readiness should re-derive independently via sensitivity_model.py, not just trust this block. The shift/fleet-capacity fields (2026-08-20 fix) resolve a real Tier 2 P2 finding: avg_long_distance/total_deliveries_day are correctly option-invariant because fleet drive-time capacity (75 vehicle-hr/day) is never the binding constraint under either option (only 42%/35% utilized) -- delivery volume is demand-bound, not speed-bound. The one genuine, quantified exception is per-route single-vehicle dedication: Option A cannot cover Eugene's 2.7/day average with one dedicated vehicle (ceiling 2/day), Option B can (ceiling 4/day) -- see balance.argument_b.

modeling_assumptions.text: Probability a driver is pulled over, given they are observed by an officer while driving 6-10 mph over the posted limit, is modeled at 25% -- carried forward from the original case's own unattributed 'recent studies' claim since no current, attributable public source breaks out pull-over probability by mph-over bracket.

Each vehicle is realistically observed by an officer positioned to act, while sustaining a 10-over habit on Inland's regular routes, roughly 8 times per year (about once every 6-7 weeks) -- a modest, stated planning assumption; no public data measures route-specific enforcement-exposure frequency.

Insurance surcharge is modeled as a single year's cost per ticket earned that year (steady-state), not stacked/compounded across the multi-year window a real insurer's look-back would apply -- a simplification disclosed as understating Option B's true multi-year cost.

Portland-area city arterial posted speed is modeled at 35 mph, per PBOT's own documented typical range (35-45 mph) for the nonresidential arterials this fleet uses, rather than Oregon's lower unposted default (20-25 mph).

sensitivity_note: The 17.26% margin is real but is directly tuned by MA1 x MA2 (probability x annual exposure frequency, both disclosed, unsourced assumptions) -- see case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5 and sensitivity_model.py. A +-50% flex on either dial moves expected tickets/vehicle/year materially and is expected to move the margin; whether it flips the winner or breaches the 20% cap is recorded in QA_REPORT.md, not asserted here. Separately, delivery-capacity is not a tunable dial: honest math across four independent allocation methods shows fleet drive-time capacity (75 vehicle-hr/day) is never the binding constraint under either option, so avg_long_distance/total_deliveries_day are correctly fixed across A and B (demand-bound). Option B's real, quantified non-cost counter is instead a per-route capacity-ceiling fact (Eugene: 2 round trips/vehicle/day under A vs. 4 under B) -- see balance.argument_b and derived{}.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The true probability of being pulled over given an officer observes a driver 6-10 mph over the limit exists in principle (it is a real quantity a police department's own dispatch/citation data could compute), but no public source publishes it broken out by mph-over bracket -- a genuine two-framing search (see RESEARCH_LOG.md P12) found only adjacent proxies (a St. Paul enforcement-threshold study, AAA Foundation self-report data). MA1's 25% is a documented good-faith estimate carried forward from the original case's own claim, not a research gap papered over.

Route-specific enforcement-exposure frequency (how often a given vehicle on Inland's specific routes is actually observed by an officer positioned to act) exists in principle inside a real police agency's own patrol-deployment data, but is not publicly accessible for any specific commercial route. MA2's 8/year is a stated, modest planning estimate, not a measured rate -- disclosed explicitly rather than presented as sourced.
